props.label: About Us
props.heading: We size it against your bill, not our stock
props.body:
Suryodaya Solar has been fitting rooftop systems around Nagpur since 2016 — houses, housing societies, schools and small factories.

The one thing we do differently is the sizing. Plenty of companies quote the system they want to sell. We read your last six bills, measure the shade-free area on your roof, and tell you the size that matches what you actually use. Sometimes that is smaller than you were expecting, and we would rather say so than sell you panels that export power you get little back for.

Our own team does the installation. No subcontractors, which means when something needs attention in year four you are calling the people who fitted it.

And we do the paperwork — net metering with MSEDCL and the PM Surya Ghar subsidy claim, followed up until the money is in your account. It is the part most people give up on, and it is included.

props.label: Solar Panels & Systems
props.heading: Panel types, and complete systems
props.sub: Four panel technologies and four system types. If you are not sure which you need, start with the Mono PERC or just send us your bill.

items.title: Mono PERC Half-Cut
items.desc: The default choice for a rooftop in India. High output, and the half-cut design keeps producing when one part of the panel is shaded by a tank or a parapet.
items.body:
If you are not sure which panel to pick, this is the one to start with.

A half-cut panel splits each cell in two and wires the halves separately. It sounds like a detail, and on an open field it barely matters — but on an Indian rooftop, where a water tank, a parapet wall or a neighbour's building shades part of the array for an hour or two a day, it is the difference between losing a little output and losing a lot.

Mono PERC cells sit around 20-21% efficiency, so you need fewer panels for the same output — which matters when the roof is only so big.

Carries a 12-year product warranty and a 25-year performance warranty from the manufacturer. We handle the claim if one ever fails.

items.title: TOPCon N-Type
items.desc: The newest cell technology we stock. Highest efficiency, best performance in Nagpur summers, and it degrades more slowly than anything else on this page.
items.body:
If your roof is small and you want the most units out of it, this is the panel.

TOPCon cells run at 22-23% efficiency, a genuine step above Mono PERC. More usefully for this part of the country, they lose less output as the panel heats up — and a rooftop panel in Nagpur in May is very hot indeed. On paper the gap is a few percent; across an afternoon in peak summer it is larger than that.

They also degrade more slowly. Most panels lose about 0.55% of their output per year; TOPCon is nearer 0.4%. Over 25 years that compounds into a meaningful difference.

It costs more per panel. Worth it when roof space is the constraint, not the budget.

items.title: Bifacial Glass-to-Glass
items.desc: Glass on both faces, so it also collects the light bouncing off your roof. Worth doing on a light-coloured terrace or an elevated structure — not on a dark tiled roof.
items.body:
A bifacial panel has glass on the back as well as the front, so it generates from light reflected off whatever is underneath it.

Be careful with this one, because the extra output depends entirely on what it is mounted over. On a white-painted terrace or an elevated structure with open ground below, you can gain 5-15%. Lying flat against a dark tiled roof with no gap, you gain almost nothing and have paid extra for glass.

We will tell you honestly which of those your roof is before you order. If it is the second, buy the Mono PERC and put the difference towards a bigger system.

The double-glass build is also more durable — no backsheet to yellow or crack, and better resistance to hail and humidity.

items.title: Polycrystalline
items.desc: Lower efficiency, lower price. Only makes sense when you have plenty of roof and a tight budget — we will say so if that is not you.
items.body:
Polycrystalline is the older technology, and we are straightforward about that.

It runs at 16-17% efficiency against 20-21% for Mono PERC, which means more panels and more roof for the same output. If your roof is generous and the budget is tight, that is a perfectly sensible trade and the panels will last just as long.

If your roof is small, this is a false economy — you will fill the space and still not reach the system size you wanted. In that case spend the extra on Mono PERC.

Most of our customers end up on Mono PERC. We stock these because for some roofs and some budgets they are genuinely the right answer.

items.title: On-Grid Rooftop System
items.desc: The complete job — panels, inverter, mounting, wiring, net metering and the subsidy paperwork. What most homes actually buy.
items.body:
This is what most people mean when they say they want solar.

An on-grid system runs alongside your existing MSEDCL connection. During the day the panels supply the house and anything spare is exported to the grid, spinning your meter backwards. At night you draw from the grid as normal. At the end of the billing cycle you pay only for the difference, which for a correctly sized system is close to nothing.

There is no battery, which is why it is the cheapest way to cut a bill — and also why it does not work during a power cut. If you want backup, look at the hybrid system instead.

WHAT IS INCLUDED: panels, a grid-tied inverter, galvanised mounting structure, DC and AC cabling, earthing, lightning arrestor, and the full net-metering application with MSEDCL. We also file your subsidy claim under the PM Surya Ghar scheme and follow it up until it lands in your account.

SIZING, ROUGHLY: 1 kW generates about 4 units a day averaged across the year in Nagpur, and needs about 80 sq ft of shade-free roof. A house using 300 units a month usually wants 2-3 kW. Send us a recent bill and we will size it properly.

items.title: Hybrid System with Battery
items.desc: On-grid savings plus backup that keeps running through a power cut. Costs more, and for most homes it is worth it only if cuts are frequent.
items.body:
A hybrid system does everything an on-grid system does, and adds a battery so the house keeps running when the grid goes down.

Be clear-eyed about the cost. The battery is the expensive part and it is the part that wears out — lithium packs are warranted for around ten years, lead-acid for far less. If your area gets a handful of short cuts a year, an on-grid system and an inverter you already own is better value.

If cuts are frequent, or you run something that genuinely cannot stop, the maths changes and this is the right system.

We size the battery to your essential load — lights, fans, router, one fridge — not the whole house. Backing up an air conditioner is possible and expensive, and we would rather tell you the number before you order than after.

productInfo.label: Net metering
productInfo.value: Yes, exports when the battery is full

items.title: Off-Grid System
items.desc: No grid connection at all — battery and panels only. For farms, borewells and sites where the line has never reached.
items.body:
An off-grid system carries the whole load on its own. There is no grid to fall back on, so the battery and the panel array both have to be sized for the worst week of the year, not the average one.

That makes it the most expensive way to buy solar per unit generated, and it is the right answer only when there genuinely is no connection — a farm pump, a borewell, a site office, a house where the line has never reached.

If you have a connection and it is simply unreliable, you want the hybrid system, not this one.

items.title: Solar Water Heater
items.desc: The cheapest solar you can buy, and it pays back fastest. Nothing to do with your electricity meter — it just stops the geyser running.
items.body:
A geyser is one of the hungriest things in an Indian home, and a solar water heater removes most of that load for a fraction of what a panel system costs.

It is a completely separate thing from rooftop panels — no inverter, no meter, no paperwork. Water runs through evacuated tubes on the roof, heats up, and sits in an insulated tank. On a clear Nagpur day it is hot by mid-morning and still warm the next dawn.

On a cloudy stretch in monsoon you will still need the backup element, and every tank we fit has one. Anyone who tells you otherwise has not lived through a Nagpur July.

For a family of four, 200 litres is the usual size and it typically pays for itself in two to three years.

props.label: Questions
props.heading: The things people ask before they commit

items.q: How much will this actually cut my bill?
items.a: For a correctly sized on-grid system, most of our residential customers end up paying only the fixed charges — usually between ₹90 and ₹300 a month against ₹3,000-₹5,000 before. It depends on how well the system size matches your usage, which is exactly what the free survey is for. We would rather show you the number from your own bills than quote you an average.

items.q: What subsidy can I get, and do you handle it?
items.a: Residential rooftop systems are eligible under the PM Surya Ghar scheme, which pays a fixed amount per kW up to a cap for systems of 3 kW and above. We register you on the National Portal, get the DISCOM approvals, submit the claim and follow it up until it is credited. We charge nothing for this and we do not take a share of it. Rates are set by the government and do change, so we will confirm the current figure at your survey.

items.q: What happens during a power cut?
items.a: An on-grid system shuts down. That is a safety rule, not a fault — it stops your panels feeding a line that a lineman may be working on. If you want power through a cut you need the hybrid system with a battery, which costs more. We will tell you plainly whether your area has enough cuts to justify it.

items.q: Will the panels damage my roof, and what about leaks?
items.a: On an RCC roof the structure is ballasted or chemically anchored and the roof is not penetrated at all. On a tiled or sheet roof we use proper flashing at every fixing. We have not caused a leak yet, and if we did it would be ours to fix.

items.q: How much roof do I need?
items.a: Roughly 80 square feet of shade-free roof per kW with Mono PERC panels, a little less with TOPCon. Shade matters more than area — a water tank or a neighbouring wall that shades the array for two hours a day changes the design and sometimes the panel choice.

items.q: What does it need in the way of maintenance?
items.a: Cleaning, mainly. Dust in this region can cost you 15-25% of your output in the dry months, and rinsing the array every few weeks recovers most of it. Beyond that it is an annual electrical check. There are no moving parts.

items.q: How long until it pays for itself?
items.a: For a residential on-grid system after subsidy, typically three to five years, then twenty more years of near-zero bills. Commercial systems are usually faster because the tariff is higher and the depreciation benefit applies.
